lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- Midpoint Review
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Aguinaldo Ballon | Lesson 16 -- Midpoint Review

listenings.text: In my research, I interview adult learners every six months. At the intermediate level, almost all of them say the same thing: I am not improving. Then I play them a recording from a year before, and they are always surprised. Their sentences are longer, their vocabulary is more precise, and they understand much more. The progress was real. It was just invisible to them. So my advice to teachers and learners is simple. Record yourself every few months, and listen to the old recordings. It is the best way to see progress that you cannot feel.

I started to study English seriously when I was forty-six, after I became the CEO of a company with American investors. The first year was exciting. The second year was terrible. I felt that I was not making any progress, and I almost stopped. My teacher did something simple. She asked me to give the same five-minute presentation I had given in my first lesson. I could not believe the difference. After that, we changed the method. Less new grammar, more real tasks from my work, and a lot of correction. Today I still make mistakes, but I chair board meetings in English without fear.

paras: Adult learners usually make fast progress in their first year of English. They learn the basic tenses, a few hundred words, and they can survive in a meeting. Then, somewhere around the intermediate level, progress seems to stop. Teachers call this the intermediate plateau. Learners describe it differently: I study, but I don't feel any better. It is one of the most common reasons why professionals give up.

Researchers say the plateau is not a lack of talent. It is a change in the type of progress. At the beginning, every new word is visible. At the intermediate level, progress happens in details: more precise vocabulary, better accuracy, faster listening. These details are harder to notice, so learners think they are not improving. Another problem is the blind spot. Many intermediate speakers have reached a level of fluency that lets them communicate, so they stop noticing their own mistakes. If nobody corrects them, the mistakes become permanent.

The good news is that the plateau can be broken. Experts recommend three things. First, take stock regularly: an honest self-assessment shows where the real gaps are. Second, choose depth over quantity: it is better to fine-tune ten structures than to learn fifty new ones. Third, value consistency: short, regular practice works better than long sessions once a month. A setback, like two weeks without classes, is normal. What matters is coming back.
